title: Object-Oriented Programming
description: Model data and behavior together using classes and objects

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Define a class, create instances (objects), and understand the class/object relationship.

sections.title: 🏗️ Defining a Class
sections.content:
A class is a blueprint; an object (instance) is a specific thing built from that blueprint.

```python
class Dog:
    pass

my_dog = Dog()      # an instance of Dog
another_dog = Dog() # a different, separate instance

type(my_dog)   # <class '__main__.Dog'>
```

sections.title: 🏷️ Instance Attributes
sections.content:
You can attach data directly to an object.

```python
my_dog.name = "Rex"
my_dog.age = 3

print(my_dog.name)   # 'Rex'
```

This works, but is fragile — the next lesson shows the proper way using `__init__`.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Confusing the class (the blueprint, e.g. `Dog`) with an instance (an actual object, e.g. `my_dog`).

questions.question: What is a class?
questions.explanation: Classes define the structure and behavior objects will have.

questions.question: What is an instance?
options: A specific object created from a class
questions.explanation: Instances are the actual objects built using the class blueprint.

questions.question: How do you create an instance of class `Dog`?
questions.explanation: Calling the class like a function creates a new instance.

questions.question: Can two instances of the same class have different attribute values?
options: Yes, each instance has its own data
questions.explanation: Each object maintains its own independent state.

questions.question: What does `type(my_dog)` show?
questions.explanation: type() reveals which class created the object.

questions.question: By convention, class names use...
questions.explanation: PEP 8 recommends CapWords for class names.

questions.question: What keyword defines a class?
questions.explanation: The class keyword starts a class definition.

questions.question: What does `pass` do inside an empty class body?
options: Acts as a placeholder so the class is syntactically valid
questions.explanation: pass avoids a syntax error when there's nothing else in the body yet.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Use `__init__` to set up instance attributes cleanly when an object is created.

sections.title: 🏗️ The __init__ Method
sections.content:
`__init__` runs automatically when you create a new instance, setting up its initial state.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.name, rex.age)   # Rex 3
```

`self` refers to the specific instance being created or used — it's always the first parameter of instance methods.

sections.title: 🔒 Class Attributes vs Instance Attributes
sections.content:
```python
class Dog:
    species = "Canis familiaris"   # class attribute — shared by ALL dogs

    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name             # instance attribute — unique per dog

a = Dog("Rex")
b = Dog("Fido")
print(a.species, b.species)   # same for both
print(a.name, b.name)         # different per instance
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting `self` as the first parameter of `__init__` (and other methods) — Python passes the instance automatically, but you must still declare it.

questions.question: When does `__init__` run?
options: Automatically when a new instance is created
questions.explanation: It's the constructor, called implicitly by Dog(...).

questions.question: What does `self` represent inside a method?
options: The specific instance the method is called on
questions.explanation: self lets methods access and modify that instance's own attributes.

questions.question: Is a class attribute shared across all instances?
options: No, each instance has its own copy always
questions.explanation: Class attributes live on the class and are shared by default.

questions.question: What creates an instance attribute?
options: Assigning to self.attr inside a method (often __init__)
questions.explanation: self.attr = value inside __init__ is the standard pattern.

questions.question: Must `self` be the first parameter of instance methods?
questions.explanation: Python automatically passes the instance as the first argument.

questions.question: What does `Dog("Rex", 3)` do given `__init__(self, name, age)`?
options: Creates a Dog with name='Rex', age=3
questions.explanation: Arguments after self map to name and age respectively.

questions.question: Can you name the constructor something other than __init__?
options: No, __init__ is the special method Python calls
questions.explanation: __init__ is a reserved 'dunder' method name Python looks for.

questions.question: If two Dog instances change their own `.name`, does it affect the other?
questions.explanation: Each instance's own attributes are separate from other instances'.

exercise.title: Create a Student Class
exercise.prompt:
Create a class called Student.

Its constructor should receive:

name
age
course

and store them as instance attributes.

Also create a class attribute:

school = "Python Academy"

Create two students:

student1 = Student("Ali", 20, "Python")
student2 = Student("Sara", 22, "Data Science")
exercise.starterCode:
class Student:
    # Create the class attribute
    school = ""

    def __init__(self, name, age, course):
        # Store the instance attributes
        pass


student1 = Student("Ali", 20, "Python")
student2 = Student("Sara", 22, "Data Science")
exercise.tests:
assert student1.name == "Ali"
assert student1.age == 20
assert student1.course == "Python"

assert student2.name == "Sara"
assert student2.age == 22
assert student2.course == "Data Science"

assert Student.school == "Python Academy"
assert student1.school == "Python Academy"
assert student2.school == "Python Academy"
exercise.hint:
Instance attributes use self:

self.name = name
self.age = age

Class attributes are defined outside __init__:

class Student:
    school = "Python Academy"

lessons.title: Methods & self
lessons.description: Give objects behavior with instance methods

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Define methods that operate on an instance's own data.

sections.title: ⚙️ Defining Methods
sections.content:
Methods are functions defined inside a class that operate on `self`.

```python
class Dog:
    def __init__(self, name, age):
        self.name = name
        self.age = age

    def bark(self):
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

    def have_birthday(self):
        self.age += 1

rex = Dog("Rex", 3)
print(rex.bark())        # 'Rex says Woof!'
rex.have_birthday()
print(rex.age)           # 4
```

sections.title: 🧮 Methods That Return vs Modify
Common mistakes
sections.content: Calling a method without parentheses, e.g. `rex.bark` instead of `rex.bark()` — that just references the method object, it doesn't run it.

questions.question: What must every instance method include as its first parameter?
questions.explanation: self is the convention for the instance reference.

questions.question: What does `rex.bark()` do vs `rex.bark`?
options: bark() calls the method; bark (no parens) just references it
questions.explanation: Parentheses are required to actually invoke a method.

questions.question: Can a method modify the instance's own attributes?
questions.explanation: Methods can freely read and update the instance's state through self.

questions.question: What does `self.age += 1` inside a method do?
questions.explanation: It updates the calling instance's own age.

questions.question: How do you call a method named `deposit` on an object `acc` with amount 50?
questions.explanation: Dot notation calls the method bound to that instance.

questions.question: What's returned by a method with no explicit return statement?
questions.explanation: Same as regular functions — no return means None.

questions.question: Is `self` a Python keyword?
options: No, it's just a strong convention
questions.explanation: You could technically name it something else, but never should.

questions.question: What kind of thing is `can_afford` in the BankAccount example?
options: A method that returns information without changing state
questions.explanation: It reads self.balance and returns a bool, without mutating anything.

exercise.title: Build a Bank Account
exercise.prompt:
Create a class called:

BankAccount

The constructor should receive an initial balance.

Add two methods:

deposit(amount)

Adds amount to the balance.

can_afford(amount)

Returns True if the balance is enough to pay the amount, otherwise False.

Example:

account = BankAccount(100)

account.deposit(50)

The balance should now be:

150

And:

account.can_afford(120)

should return:

True
exercise.tests:
account = BankAccount(100)

assert account.balance == 100

account.deposit(50)
assert account.balance == 150

assert account.can_afford(120) == True
assert account.can_afford(200) == False
exercise.hint:
Modify an attribute with:

self.balance += amount

A method can return a comparison:

return self.balance >= amount

lessons.title: Inheritance
lessons.description: Build new classes from existing ones

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Create a subclass that extends a parent class and overrides methods.

sections.title: 🧬 Basic Inheritance
sections.content:
A subclass inherits all the attributes and methods of its parent class.

```python
class Animal:
    def __init__(self, name):
        self.name = name

    def speak(self):
        return f"{self.name} makes a sound"

class Dog(Animal):        # Dog inherits from Animal
    def speak(self):        # overrides the parent's method
        return f"{self.name} says Woof!"

rex = Dog("Rex")
print(rex.speak())   # 'Rex says Woof!' (uses Dog's version)
```

sections.title: 🔗 Using super()
sections.content:
`super()` lets a subclass call its parent's version of a method — handy for extending rather than fully replacing behavior.

```python
class Cat(Animal):
    def speak(self):
        base = super().speak()   # call Animal's speak()
        return base + " (meow-ish)"
```

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to call `super().__init__(...)` in a subclass's `__init__`, which skips setup the parent class expects to happen.

questions.question: What does `class Dog(Animal):` mean?
questions.explanation: The parenthesized name is the parent (base) class.

questions.question: What does overriding a method mean?
options: Defining a same-named method in the subclass that replaces the parent's
questions.explanation: The subclass's version takes precedence when called on its instances.

questions.question: What does `super()` give access to?
questions.explanation: super() is used to reach up to the parent implementation.

questions.question: If Dog doesn't define `__init__`, what happens when you create `Dog("Rex")`?
questions.explanation: Inheritance means unoverridden methods (including __init__) come from the parent.

questions.question: Why call `super().__init__(...)` in a subclass?
options: To run the parent's setup logic too
questions.explanation: It ensures the parent class's initialization still happens.

questions.question: Can a subclass add new methods not in the parent?
questions.explanation: Subclasses can freely extend behavior beyond the parent.

questions.question: In the Cat example, what does `super().speak()` return?
questions.explanation: super() explicitly calls up to the parent's implementation.

questions.question: Inheritance primarily supports...
questions.explanation: It lets you build on and specialize existing behavior.

exercise.title: Employee and Manager
exercise.prompt:
Create a parent class:

Employee

Its constructor should receive:

name
salary

Create a method:

get_info()

that returns:

Ali earns 5000

Then create:

Manager(Employee)

The Manager constructor should also receive:

department

Use super().__init__() to initialize name and salary.

Override get_info() so that it returns:

Sara manages IT and earns 8000
exercise.tests:
employee = Employee("Ali", 5000)
manager = Manager("Sara", 8000, "IT")

assert employee.get_info() == "Ali earns 5000"

assert manager.name == "Sara"
assert manager.salary == 8000
assert manager.department == "IT"

assert manager.get_info() == "Sara manages IT and earns 8000"

assert isinstance(manager, Employee)
exercise.hint:
Call the parent constructor using:

super().__init__(name, salary)

Then:

self.department = department

lessons.title: Polymorphism & Special Methods
lessons.description: Use dunder methods to make your classes behave like built-ins

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Implement `__str__` and `__eq__`, and understand polymorphism through a shared interface.

sections.title: 🎭 Polymorphism
✨ Special (Dunder) Methods
Common mistakes
sections.content: Forgetting to define `__eq__` and then being surprised that `p1 == p2` compares object identity (memory address) instead of the values you care about.

questions.question: What is polymorphism?
options: Different classes responding to the same method call in their own way
Having many classes in one file
questions.explanation: The same interface, different underlying behavior.

questions.question: What does `__str__` control?
options: What print()/str() display for an object
Whether the object can be compared
questions.explanation: Defining __str__ customizes the human-readable representation.

questions.question: What does `__eq__` control?
options: Behavior of the == operator for that class
questions.explanation: Without __eq__, == compares by identity, not by value.

questions.question: Without a custom `__eq__`, what does `==` compare by default?
options: Object identity (are they the same object in memory)
questions.explanation: The default equality check is identity-based unless overridden.

questions.question: What are methods like `__init__` and `__str__` commonly called?
questions.explanation: Their double-underscore naming gives them the nickname 'dunder'.

questions.question: In the polymorphism example, why does `animal.speak()` behave differently for each object?
options: Each class defines its own version of speak()
questions.explanation: Each class's own method implementation is what's called.

questions.question: What does `str(p1)` do if `__str__` is defined?
questions.explanation: str() delegates to the object's __str__ method.

questions.question: Why implement dunder methods on your own classes?
options: To make your objects work naturally with built-in functions/operators
questions.explanation: Dunder methods integrate custom classes with Python's built-in behavior.

exercise.title: Create a Product Class
exercise.prompt:
Create a class called:

Product

Its constructor receives:

name
price

Implement __str__ so:

product = Product("Laptop", 3500)
print(product)

displays:

Laptop - $3500

Then implement __eq__ so two products are considered equal when their name and price are both equal.
exercise.tests:
p1 = Product("Laptop", 3500)
p2 = Product("Laptop", 3500)
p3 = Product("Phone", 2000)

assert str(p1) == "Laptop - $3500"

assert p1 == p2
assert not (p1 == p3)
exercise.hint:
For __str__:

return f"{self.name} - ${self.price}"

For equality:

return self.name == other.name and self.price == other.price

challenge.title: Polymorphism
challenge.prompt:
Given:

class Dog:
    def speak(self):
        return "Woof"


class Cat:
    def speak(self):
        return "Meow"

Create:

animals = [Dog(), Cat()]

Use one loop:

for animal in animals:

and call the same:

animal.speak()

on both objects.

Expected output:

Woof
Meow
